Key Terms.definition: Memory is made of three stores (sensory, short-term, long-term), and information moves between them in a fixed order.
Repeating information to keep it in short-term memory and move it into long-term memory.
Grouping items into larger meaningful units, such as a phone number in three parts, so more fits in short-term memory.
Long-term memory for facts and general knowledge.
Long-term memory for how to do things, such as riding a bike.
A mental framework built from past experience that we use to rebuild memories, which can distort them.
A question worded so that it pushes the person toward a particular answer.

Theories & Researchers.name: Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968)
Theories & Researchers.summary: Multi-store model: information passes from sensory memory to short-term memory if attended to, and into long-term memory through rehearsal.

Theories & Researchers.name: Miller (1956)
Theories & Researchers.summary: Short-term memory holds about 7 plus or minus 2 items, and chunking helps stretch this.

Theories & Researchers.name: Bartlett
Theories & Researchers.summary: Reconstructive memory: we rebuild memories using schemas instead of replaying a recording, so they get distorted.

Key Studies.method: Participants saw trigrams such as XPJ, then counted backwards in threes so they could not rehearse.
Key Studies.findings: After 18 seconds only about 10% were recalled, suggesting short-term memory decays quickly without rehearsal.

Key Studies.method: 45 students watched car crash clips, then estimated speed with the verb changed in the question (smashed, collided, bumped, hit, contacted).
Key Studies.findings: Smashed gave 40.5 mph and contacted gave 31.8 mph. A week later 32% of the smashed group reported broken glass, against 14% of the hit group.

Evaluation: Multi-store model is too simple: patient KF had damaged short-term memory but could still form long-term memories, so short-term memory may have more than one part.
Rehearsal is not the only way information reaches long-term memory.
Peterson & Peterson used meaningless trigrams, so the study has low ecological validity.
Loftus & Palmer was a lab study with video clips, so participants were less stressed than real witnesses. It was well controlled and easy to replicate.
Real-World Examples: Police should ask a witness 'was there a weapon?' instead of 'did you see the knife?' to avoid leading questions.
Remembering exam content better when you sit in the same room where you learned it.
Testing yourself works better for revision than rereading.

Quiz Yourself.q: What are the three stores in the multi-store model?
Quiz Yourself.a: Sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory.

Quiz Yourself.q: What did Peterson & Peterson stop their participants from doing by making them count backwards?
In Loftus & Palmer, which verb led to the highest speed estimates?
Give one criticism of the multi-store model.
Quiz Yourself.a: It is too simple: short-term memory is not a single store, as patient KF showed, and rehearsal is not the only route to long-term memory.
